findings.title: The marked tokens occur in unrelated snippets and include varied name fragments, numbers, and common words, with no clear shared pattern or function.
This pole strongly tracks real-estate title insurance terminology and FAQ text, especially “title policy,” “title insurance,” and related coverage.
Mostly varied grammatical continuations—prepositions, conjunctions, auxiliaries, and occasional content words—with no consistent semantic or syntactic pattern beyond ordinary sentence flow.
Often marks additive or alternative enumeration (and/or, commas, both, more), though several examples are ordinary unrelated function words.
Fires on components of structured, code-like strings—account numbers, citations, IDs, URLs, phone numbers, dates, and product codes—rather than ordinary quantities.
Fires on numbers and number-like labels used as ordinary quantities, measurements, list items, or descriptive headings in prose.
Fires on “spandex” in clothing, accessories, and product descriptions, typically as a stretch-fabric material or ingredient.
Fires on references to Sylvia Plath and, separately, on “pull out” phrases or pull-out features; these patterns appear unrelated.
Often marks a continuation that elaborates on a noun or group—by giving an example, appositive, relative clause, or another item in a list.
Strongly associated with the second-person pronoun “you,” especially when directly addressing or emphasizing the reader or a loved one.
Mostly marks “Agence France-Presse” in news credits and copyright footers; a few unrelated acronym, name, and citation fragments make the pattern less consistent.
Clusters around compact numeric references, especially Bible chapter-and-verse citations, with a few similar road-number and DOI strings; the formatting, not theology, appears salient.
The firings lean toward ordinary concrete vocabulary about food, ingredients, and practical tools, but the examples are too varied to establish one consistent semantic trigger.
The pole favors capitalized plural terms used as proper names or labels—especially “Stars,” “Oaks,” and “Americans”—with a few noisy cases.

Fires on distinctive whole words or subword chunks in uncommon technical terms and proper names, often near the end of a compound; conservation-related passages recur, but no single topic explains all examples.
Fires on fragments from unrelated items—chickenpox, Linus, and scripture verse numbers—with no clear shared linguistic or topical function beyond occurring inside or beside words and numerals.
Fires on “Leo” as the zodiac sign and as a personal or historical name, with occasional constellation references; the shared pattern is the word itself.
Fires on digits within numbers beginning with 15, mostly sixteenth-century dates but also phone numbers, codes, and measurements.
Marks the continuation of hyphenated compounds, including lexical compounds, phrases, and transliterated terms.
Marks text immediately following a comma, including ordinary clause continuations, parentheticals, and dates.
Several examples pair “civil” with institutional terms such as “court” or “protection,” but many others are unrelated names or word fragments, so no consistent broader pattern is clear.
Strongly fires on “Civil War” and related historical or political discussion of armed civil conflicts, including passages about Cromwell and other wars.
Marks quantified temporal spans, especially in “for over/for nearly/for several” constructions describing how long something has lasted or been true.
Marks varied non-duration continuations of “for,” such as beneficiaries, purposes, objects, and circumstances, contrasting with the positive pole’s duration phrases.
The firings span unrelated color names, ordinary nouns, word fragments, and proper-name components, with no stable semantic or structural pattern evident.
Most firings mark “side” in regional names and compounds such as Teesside, Wearside, sell-side, riverside, and gulfside; a few geographic terms and names are outliers.
Fires on generic nouns that frame a setting or circumstance—especially “place” and “case,” but also “service” and “room”—often in reviews or explanatory phrases.
Fires around named destinations and public or institutional venues, often in phrases like “to the beach,” “the ER,” or “the nurse’s office.”
Centers on “go,” especially in compound expressions such as grab-and-go, get-up-and-go, and stop-and-go; a few scattered activations do not fit this pattern.
Strongly favors references to the Open University and, more broadly, names beginning with “Open”; a few weaker examples appear unrelated.
Fires on punctuation, separators, and isolated characters at textual seams, often amid line breaks, formatting oddities, or OCR-like corruption; no consistent subject matter appears.
Fires on ellipses and similar excerpt boundaries where scraped text is visibly truncated or omitted, including cut-off listings, descriptions, and search results.
Marks calendar-time references, especially retrospective anniversaries phrased as “this month/week” and components of formatted dates.
Most clearly marks the digit 9 inside birth-year strings; the remaining examples are scattered words without a coherent shared pattern.
Fires on commas after sentence adverbs and other transitionals or parenthetical modifiers, such as “therefore,” “hence,” “hopefully,” and “in particular.”
Fires around discourse interruptions and asides, especially hesitation fillers like “er” and “um,” but also punctuation after transitions such as “therefore” and “though.”
Marks an incidental consequence or secondary outcome—literal or metaphorical—often in the phrases “side effect” and “by-product.”
Marks informal conversational “like” as a filler or discourse connector, and as a comparison or approximation introducing an example or thought.
Fires on tokens forming or completing proper names—people, places, titles, products, and organizations—often at a name’s wordpiece boundary.
Fires on numbered hierarchical labels, especially Layer 2/3 and L2/L3 networking references, with similar Level 2/3 labels in other contexts.
Often fires on nominal material completing an “of” phrase, including heads and modifiers, though some examples are less direct.
The marked tokens range from conjunctions and relative “that” to unrelated content words, with no consistent shared pattern.
The marked items range from ordinary verbs and function words to punctuation and corrupted text across unrelated contexts, with no reliable shared pattern.
The pole often marks symbols or fragments in technical, mathematical, engineering, and structured data contexts, though a few examples are unrelated.
Favors distinctive proper-name and brand fragments—especially people, organizations, and products—with a few unrelated numeric or ordinary-word exceptions.
Often marks ordinary catalog or informational vocabulary, especially “shareware,” but “avoidance,” “School,” and “Grove” do not form a clear narrower theme.
Primarily fires on “oldie/oldies,” especially nostalgic songs, recipes, or familiar favorites; scattered matches in Oldenburg, oldid, and names look incidental.
Often fires on “Old Man” in names, titles, and descriptions, but also on “Cadbury” and “old lady,” with no clear shared pattern.
It primarily fires on “make room” constructions, including figurative space for people, plans, or things, with a few related make/create expressions.
The marked words occur in unrelated contexts, from “donation” and “cameo” to “switch” and “intercession,” with no clear shared pattern.
Fires mainly on expressions that quantify or compare amounts, such as “number/amount/total of,” “a pair of,” and “as many as,” with a few incidental collocations.
Often marks exhaustive “all [person] …” formulations that explain the sole thing someone needs, wants, or can do; several examples are less consistent function-word contexts.
